svg.title: One page of MCP, revision 2026-07-28, drawn by hand
svg.desc: A hand-drawn single-sheet reference for the Model Context Protocol at revision 2026-07-28, laid out in eight panels. It covers the three roles of host, client and server; the three primitives and who triggers each; the shape of a self-describing request and its reserved metadata keys; the full method list including what was removed; the result types and the multi round-trip request loop that replaced the server-to-client channel; the split between protocol errors and tool execution errors; the two transports; and a short security checklist. Same panel layout as the printed poster, so the two can be read side by side.
svg.text: Model Context Protocol, revision 2026-07-28. The revision where the protocol became stateless.
HOST — owns the model, the conversation, and consent
Nothing is negotiated first, so everything travels per request.
protocolVersion and clientCapabilities are REQUIRED on every request.
clientInfo, logLevel, serverInfo, subscriptionId are optional.
progressToken, traceparent, tracestate, baggage carry no prefix.
5 · There is no back channel. A server that needs input returns, and is retried.
This is MRTR, the multi round-trip request. It replaced every server-to-client request.
The client handles it. The model never sees it.
A successful response. Fed back so the model can retry.
stdout IS the protocol. Log to stderr, never print.
No session, so round-robin balancing just works.
8 · Six things the protocol will not do for you
1 · Tool descriptions are untrusted input to the model.
Injection lands at tools/list, before any approval prompt fires.
2 · Annotations are hints. readOnlyHint enforces nothing.
3 · Never accept a token not issued for you. Never forward one upstream.
4 · Validate Origin. Bind local servers to 127.0.0.1.
5 · Resource template variables are untrusted. Use an allowlist.
6 · Private data + untrusted content + an outbound channel
is the lethal trifecta. Remove one of the three.
What The Hell is MCP — a free 24-post series. Prose CC-BY 4.0, code MIT.
